full_judgment:
28. Once the existence of improper inducement is established so as to bring the case within the purview of section 24 of the Evidence Act, there is a presumption of the continuance of such inducement, promise or threat and it is the duty of the prosecution to satisfy the Court that the impression caused by the original inducement had been fully removed. See Nazir vs State (PLD 1960 Lah. 189). There is no material on the record to show that the impression had been removed from the mind of Muhammad Ramzan appellant at the time of his making the statement. We, therefore, rule it out of consideration." 

 32. In our jurisdiction, their Lordships in the case of Sate vs Tayeb Ali reported in 40 DLR (AD)(188) 6 held that suspicion is not substitute of evidence. In the case of Osman Gani vs State, 2001 BLT (AD) 107 their Lordships held that suspicion, however, strong cannot be the basis of conviction. It has been held in the case of Md. Ali Haider vs State, 40 DLR 97 that probability however strong, and suspicion however grave, can never take place of proof as because in a criminal trial presumption of innocence is a principle of cardinal importance and so guilt of the accused must be proved beyond reasonable doubt by legal, reliable and un-impeachable evidence. We wholeheartedly endorse the aforesaid decisions saying once again that suspicion and probability, however strong and grave, can never take place of proof.
